paras: The killing of Bill Williams, also reported as Jim Titus, was the fatal shooting of a Black escaped convict by Memphis police sergeant James Scott at a cabin near Overton station, Tennessee, in mid-January 1882. The officers said he attacked them with an ax when they forced the door, and they left his body where it fell. The Memphis Daily Appeal told the story at length from the officers' side, while papers in Georgia, Texas, Missouri and Mississippi carried a one-sentence wire item.

According to the Appeal, Williams had been arrested over a year earlier for shooting Monroe Alexander and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He worked for several months on 'Eusley's plantation' (in wire copy 'Ensley's farm') before escaping, and the Appeal said he set fire to a storehouse as he left. Police had been looking for him for six months, though a Dallas condensation put the escape about six weeks earlier.

On the afternoon of January 14, by the Appeal's account, Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler took a Chesapeake and Ohio train to Overton station, about six miles from Memphis, and walked about three miles east to the shanty of a Black man named Cousins. A voice inside refused to let them in, saying the owner had told him to admit nobody, and on Scott's order Butler pushed in the door. The officers said an ax blow cut the rim of Butler's hat, Butler's cartridge misfired, and Williams then ran out slashing at Scott, cutting his trousers.

Scott shot him, and Williams ran some twenty yards and fell dead. Because it was a 'colored neighborhood' and they expected the residents to rise, the officers hurried back to the station without the body and reached the Memphis stationhouse that night 'covered with mud'.
No report of an inquest, a recovery of the body, or any statement from Cousins or other residents appears in the coverage.

The Appeal ran the story under the headline 'An Officer's Shot', with decks calling Williams a 'Worthless Negro Convict' who tried to 'brain' the officers. Its text praised the sergeant for taking aim 'coolly', mocked the death with the phrase 'fell with a dull thud', and called the neighbors the officers expected to confront 'dusky recreants'.

A Memphis dispatch dated January 15 reached the Savannah Morning News and the Waco Daily Examiner, reporting that Jim Titus, alias Bill Williams, 'colored', was killed 'while resisting arrest' ten miles north of Memphis. The Dallas Daily Herald condensed it further, saying only that he refused to surrender and the officers shot him. A 'Personal and General' column item naming the sergeant as James Scott ran in the Richmond Democrat, the Iron County Register and the Grenada Sentinel through January 28.

The wire's January 15 dateline and 'this afternoon' conflict with the Appeal's Jan. 15 report that the shooting happened 'yesterday afternoon'; the local paper, which had the officers' own return that night, points to January 14. The papers also differ on distance, the Appeal placing the cabin about nine miles' travel from the city by train and foot and the wire placing the killing ten miles north of Memphis.

reader.title: Killing of Bill Williams (Jim Titus)
bases: Two Memphis police officers sent to recapture an escaped convict shot and killed him at a cabin near Overton station; no crowd took part (A1, A2).

The Memphis Appeal's local report and a separately worded Memphis wire agree that Police Sergeant Scott shot and killed the escaped convict while trying to arrest him (A1, A2, A3), though every account rests on the officers' version.

accounts.label: Officers' account (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: Williams refused to open the door, swung an ax at Butler when the door was forced and then slashed at Scott, who shot him; the officers fled the 'colored neighborhood' leaving the body.

accounts.label: Memphis wire
accounts.gist: Jim Titus, alias Bill Williams, a colored escaped convict, was shot and killed by Sergeant Scott while resisting arrest ten miles north of Memphis.

accounts.label: Condensed telegram (Dallas)
accounts.gist: He refused to surrender when found, and the officers shot him; escaped about six weeks earlier.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'An Officer's Shot' ending 'a Worthless Negro Convict', said the sergeant 'coolly took aim', and called the aroused neighbors 'dusky recreants'.
Out-of-town papers ran a one-sentence wire or column item, 'A Convict Shot' or 'Convict Killed', framed as resisting arrest.
